hops.title: Apollo astronauts who saw light that was not there
hops.text: In July 1969, Buzz Aldrin told the Apollo 11 debriefing that he had seen little flashes and streaks of light inside the cabin when no light was there. Astronauts on later flights, through Apollo 17, reported the same thing, which researchers tentatively attributed to heavy cosmic-ray nuclei passing through their heads and eyes. In the early 1970s, physicists tested this by putting their own dark-adapted eyes into low-intensity particle accelerator beams, and saw flashes on cue. Ethical concerns now rule that out. A speeding atomic nucleus is not light, but once it excites the retina, the optic nerve carries the signal to the brain as light.

sources.citation: Narici L. Light flashes and other sensory illusions perceived in space travel and on ground, including proton and heavy ion therapies. Z Med Phys. 2024;34(1):44-63.
Pinsky LS, Osborne WZ, Bailey JV, Benson RE, Thompson LF. Light flashes observed by astronauts on Apollo 11 through Apollo 17. Science. 1974;183(4128):957-959.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An astronaut seen from behind resting in a fully dark spacecraft cabin, with faint white streaks seeming to hover just before their eyes.
image.caption: Cosmic rays that excite the retina are seen as flashes, because optic nerve activity is read as light.

hops.title: Fractures and cavities that exist only in the viewer's eye
hops.text: On a neck X-ray, a dark line often crosses the base of the dens, a small peg on the second neck vertebra. In 1977, radiologist Richard Daffner warned that this common band is a Mach band that can be mistaken for a fracture, and that the mistake could put a trauma patient into skeletal traction for nothing. Dentists see the same thing beside a bright filling, where a dark rim can pass for decay. Densitometer tracings show the film is no darker there. Lateral inhibition, a bright neighbour suppressing the signal beside it, is thought to be part of why the eye exaggerates such borders.

sources.citation: Daffner RH. Pseudofracture of the dens: Mach bands. AJR Am J Roentgenol. 1977;128(4):607-612.
Lane EJ, Proto AV, Phillips TW. Mach bands and density perception. Radiology. 1976;121(1):9-17.
Yeung AWK. The diagnostic relevance and interfaces covered by Mach band effect in dentistry: an analysis of the literature. Healthcare. 2022;10(4):632.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A glowing light box on a desk showing a grayscale dental X-ray of one molar with a bright filling, beside a magnifying glass.
image.caption: Beside a bright filling, the eye can paint a dark rim that looks like decay but is not there.

hops.afterHeading: Lines or patterns: coding what kind of stimulus
hops.title: How a 1942 graph helped spread the tongue map
hops.text: Many people learned a tongue map in school: sweet at the tip, salty and sour on the sides, bitter at the back. A misread graph probably spread it. In 1901, the German researcher David Hänig measured taste thresholds for sweet, sour, salty and bitter along the tongue's edge and found only small differences. In 1942, the American psychologist Edwin Boring replotted those data as relative curves that hid how small the differences were. Later authors read the dips as almost no sensation. In fact, cells for each basic taste are spread across the tongue. Where taste runs on dedicated cells, the line is set by cell type, not by place.

sources.citation: Spence C. The tongue map and the spatial modulation of taste perception. Curr Res Food Sci. 2022;5:598-610.
Chandrashekar J, Hoon MA, Ryba NJ, Zuker CS. The receptors and cells for mammalian taste. Nature. 2006;444(7117):288-294.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A strawberry, a lemon wedge, sea salt and dark chocolate on a wooden board beside a blank rolled-up map.
image.caption: A misread 1942 graph probably helped spread the tongue map; every basic taste is detected across the tongue.
